nameStory: The showy lady's slipper gets its name from its spectacular inflated pouch that looks just like a delicate pink and white slipper fit for royalty. The 'showy' part is well-deserved – this is considered one of North America's most beautiful wildflowers. Its scientific name 'reginae' means 'of the queen,' earning it the nickname 'queen's lady's-slipper.'
description: The showy lady's slipper is a stunning wild orchid that stands 1-4 feet tall with a single magnificent flower crowning each stem. The flower features a puffy, pouch-like 'slipper' that's white with pink streaks or solid rose-pink, topped by white petals streaked with pink veins. Large, deeply ribbed leaves clasp the sturdy stem, and the whole plant has a robust, almost tropical appearance despite thriving in northern climates. This is one of New England's rarest and most spectacular wildflowers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single large flower with an inflated white pouch streaked or flushed with pink, topped by white sepals and petals with pink veining – unmistakable slipper shape about 2 inches across

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: 3-5 large oval leaves with deep parallel ridges running lengthwise, clasping the stem alternately – feel deeply pleated and somewhat fuzzy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single sturdy stem 1-4 feet tall, usually growing in small colonies – much taller and more robust than the common pink lady's slipper

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thick, hairy stem that feels soft and downy – the hairs can cause skin irritation in sensitive people, so look but don't touch

habitat: Found in cool, moist areas like cedar swamps, wet meadows, boggy woods, and along stream edges where the soil stays consistently damp. Prefers alkaline conditions and is often associated with northern white cedar, tamarack, and other moisture-loving trees. In New England, look for it in calcareous wetlands and rich, mucky soils.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge in May, growing rapidly from the rich wetland soil as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Blooms in late June through July with its spectacular pink and white slippers – peak viewing is usually early to mid-July in New England.
seasonality.fall: Leaves yellow and die back by September, leaving little trace above ground as the plant retreats to its underground rhizome.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no visible parts above ground – the thick rhizome waits beneath the soil and snow.

funFact: This orchid can take up to 16 years to bloom for the first time and may live for over 100 years, making each flowering plant you see potentially older than your grandparents!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with the much more common pink lady's slipper, but the showy lady's slipper is much taller (3+ feet vs. under 1 foot), has multiple large leaves on the stem (not just two basal leaves), and blooms much later in summer. Memory trick: 'Showy is tall and late, pink is small and early.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'pink lady's-slipper' in some regions, this is completely different from the common pink lady's slipper that blooms in spring. The showy lady's slipper is Minnesota's state flower but has become extremely rare throughout most of its range due to habitat destruction and over-collection.
compareHints: Unlike the pink lady's slipper which has two basal leaves and a solid pink pouch, the showy lady's slipper has multiple stem leaves and a white pouch with pink markings. It's much larger than the yellow lady's slipper and blooms later than both relatives. The ram's-head lady's slipper has a distinctly different pouch shape that resembles a ram's head rather than a rounded slipper.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pink lady's slipper is the only lady's slipper orchid in New England with just two basal leaves and a pink pouch.
Yellow lady's slipper is the only bright yellow slipper orchid in New England.
Ram's-head is much smaller than its lady's slipper relatives and has unique twisted petals that spiral backward like ribbons.
